transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-05 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Jonah Mills (Redwood SE), Mark Holloway (CTO, BriarCove), Lina Ortega (Head of Infra), Ben Park (Network), Sara Kim (Security)

Summary:
Customer evaluating Redwood Private for on-prem/VPC deployment. Key focus: egress & bandwidth caps, region residency for EU customers, enterprise SOC/compliance needs, and whether Dedicated vs Private makes sense. They have a hybrid cloud model and strict egress controls.

Topics:
- VPC peering vs Private Endpoints vs Transit Gateway
- Egress IPs, NAT, and firewall rules
- Bandwidth profiling and expected peak tokens/sec
- Private control plane (air-gapped) vs managed private plane
- SOC2, KMS integration, SAML SSO, audit logs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE. We'll do a quick run through your network constraints and then dive into some technical details. Priya and Jonah are here for the deep nitty-gritty.
[00:18] Mark Holloway: Hey Alex, thanks. We'll try to keep this tight. We're evaluating a private deployment or dedicated reserved capacity. Main ask: we need to understand egress and how much outbound traffic to expect, and how to lock it down to our private IP ranges.
[00:32] Priya Raman: Cool. Quick clarification, when you say private deployment do you mean deploying Redwood Private inside your VPC or an on-prem air-gapped option?
[00:40] Lina Ortega: We're mostly VPC-first. We have a co-lo that hosts sensitive workloads; some parts are on AWS GovCloud for certain customers. So ideally VPC peering or PrivateLink style endpoints. Air-gapped might be future.
[00:56] Ben Park: And the firewall team is strict: only specific egress IPs, port lists and also strict TLS inspection rules. We need to know static IPs or ranges if possible.
[01:10] Jonah Mills: Understood. Redwood Private supports private endpoints and also routing via transit gateway. You can pin egress to a NAT or a set of static egress IPs if you run our collector in your VPC or use our private egress nodes.
[01:22] Mark Holloway: Collector? Sorry, can you run that part again?
[01:26] Priya Raman: Yeah, jargonfy: we have an optional data plane component that sits in the customer's VPC and proxies model calls to the runtime. If you host the data plane, outbound egress is your IP space. If you use Redwood-managed private egress, we give you a set of static IP blocks that you can firewall to.
[01:47] Sara Kim: Is that the control plane talking home? We can't have model data leaving country X for EU-only customers.
[01:54] Alex Chen: Good callout. Control plane is separate: Redwood Private offers a customer-managed control plane option where the control plane is in your VPC — no control-plane metadata leaves your VPC. For hosted control plane, we log telemetry to Redwood, but we can support region-restricted control planes. We'll include the exact flow in the diagram.
[02:12] Ben Park: So in the hosted egress case, will you provide ASN or IP prefixes we can submit to our firewall? We need stable objects for rulesets.
[02:22] Priya Raman: Yes, for managed egress we publish stable egress IP ranges per-region. There's a small caveat: if you need absolute IP fixity we recommend the customer-hosted data plane approach.
[02:33] Mark Holloway: What's the difference in latency/cost between customer-hosted data plane vs Redwood-managed private egress?
[02:40] Jonah Mills: If you host the data plane in the same VPC or AZ as your services, latency is lower — you avoid an extra network hop. Cost-wise, you take on the egress cost and running the data plane, but you avoid inter-region traffic. Managed egress might add cross-AZ hops in some deployments. We'll provide profiling in the pilot.
[02:56] Sara Kim: On compliance — do you have SOC2? ISO? KMS integration? We need to map those into our audit.
[03:03] Alex Chen: We are SOC2 Type II and have ISO certificates — I'll include the certs. For KMS, Redwood Private supports external KMS and HSM integration for model keys and customer data keys. We'll share details on supported providers.
[03:18] Lina Ortega: Good. Also curious about SSO — SAML or OIDC? RBAC?
[03:23] Priya Raman: Both SAML and OIDC supported. RBAC with role mappings, audit logs shipped to CloudWatch or sent to your SIEM via syslog — we can push detailed request/response traces but those can be redacted for PII.
[03:38] Ben Park: Bandwidth: we have a typical inference workload right now of about 300 requests per second peak, average payload 5kB request + 12kB response. Those are rough. We need to convert that to tokens and per-minute egress for your runtime.
[03:56] Jonah Mills: Great, that's concrete. Rough rule of thumb: tokenization depends on prompt density but as an estimate, 17-20 characters per token, so you'd probably see X tokens per request. But more useful is bytes on the wire. For 300 rps with 17kB total that's about 4.8MB/s or ~345Mbps sustained at peak, plus bursts. Also consider KV cache warmups.
[04:22] Mark Holloway: We do have bursts during market openings — short spikes of 2-3x sustained for 30-60 seconds. Can Redwood handle burst capacity without dropping keys or tail latency skyrocketing?
[04:35] Priya Raman: Yes, we support autoscaling policies and can configure warm workers for spikes. On Private you can set burst capacity or keep a small warm pool to handle the opening spikes. We'll propose sizing.
[04:46] Sara Kim: For EU-only customers, all inference must remain in eu-west-1 or eu-central-1. Can the runtime be pinned to those regions and block other regions?
[04:56] Alex Chen: Absolutely — you can pin deployments to regions and force routing policies to keep traffic in-region. We also support residency tags and rollout policies to prevent cross-region fallback unless explicitly allowed.
[05:09] Ben Park: How do you do VPC peering vs PrivateLink? We prefer PrivateLink because it avoids route table changes, but peering is simpler for some of our older accounts.
[05:20] Jonah Mills: Both supported. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is generally recommended for secure, stable private connectivity and simplifies egress NATing. Transit Gateway useful if you have a hub-and-spoke with many VPCs. We'll map options to your infra.
[05:33] Lina Ortega: Any special ports we need to open? Our security team blocks uncommon ports by default.
[05:39] Priya Raman: HTTPS on 443 for control plane. For the data plane you can run over 443 too. For internal health/sample telemetry we might need a couple of ephemeral ports if you self-host the runtime; we'll list exact port ranges in the diagram.
[05:52] Mark Holloway: Ok, let's talk about persistent connections. We run long-polling streams for agents. Do you support streaming tokens over a single connection and how does that affect egress accounting?
[06:03] Jonah Mills: Yes streaming is supported over HTTP/2 or websockets. Egress accounting is bytes transmitted, so a persistent connection reduces TLS handshake overhead. For many small responses streaming reduces bandwidth slightly, but larger payloads are proportional to tokens.
[06:18] Ben Park: On IP addressing, if we do a managed egress can you commit to a maximum number of public IPs per customer? Our firewall team can't handle a huge range.
[06:29] Priya Raman: We typically allocate a small set of egress IPs per tenant; for enterprise accounts we can negotiate very small CIDR blocks or use NAT in your VPC so you can present one IP externally. We'll surface options.
[06:41] Sara Kim: What about TLS interception? Our DLP inspects HTTPS. Will Redwood tolerate TLS middleboxes?
[06:49] Alex Chen: We recommend terminating TLS inside the VPC when you host the data plane. For managed egress, TLS must be end-to-end; interception would break cert pinning. We can provide flexibility but generally avoid man-in-the-middle proxies.
[07:03] Mark Holloway: Let's go back to cost tradeoffs. If we run Private in our VPC, what's the rough cost split between Redwood and us? E.g., CPU/GPU, data transfer, licensing?
[07:12] Jonah Mills: With customer-hosted data plane + Private runtime you pay for the runtime license + support to Redwood and for the infra (GPU instances, storage, egress). For Dedicated/reserved capacity Redwood provides the infrastructure and charges monthly commitments. Hosted is pure usage. We'll model costs in the pilot — we'll ask for a 30-day traffic sample to estimate.
[07:33] Mark Holloway: For procurement, our legal will need an indemnity clause and details around data deletion. How do you handle model artifacts and logs at rest?
[07:43] Priya Raman: We can purge logs on a cadence and provide guarantees for retention windows. Key material can be kept only in your KMS, and we can provide deletion receipts for model snapshots if needed. We'll include the data flow sheet.
[07:58] Ben Park: A very practical question: if we do Private behind Transit Gateway, will the runtime manage route table sizes? We have thousands of routes in some accounts.
[08:07] Jonah Mills: We try to avoid per-ENI routes by using prefix lists and interface endpoints. Transit Gateway simplifies the scale. We'll share an example configuration that minimizes route bloat.
[08:18] Alex Chen: A quick check — is there an internal deadline or procurement timeline you're aiming at?
[08:23] Mark Holloway: We're targetting a pilot by end of Q4, procurement signoff in Q1. So a pilot in October/November would be ideal.
[08:32] Alex Chen: Great. We'll aim to get the SOC2 and network diagram to you by Wednesday, and schedule a lab benchmark the following week.
[08:40] Priya Raman: On the technical assay, can we take a quick look at your model sizes and typical token generation lengths so we can recommend quant and batching configs?
[08:48] Lina Ortega: Sure — we use a mix of an in-house GPT-2 fork for simple paraphrase tasks and a heavier 7B family model for completions. Average output length is usually 256 tokens, peaks to 1k tokens during some runs.
[09:02] Jonah Mills: That helps. For 1k output peaks you want to ensure KV cache memory coverage. We'll propose instance types and quant profiles — int8 might be fine for many workloads but any fidelity-sensitive generation we recommend int16 or bfloat where available.
[09:17] Mark Holloway: On fallbacks — if your primary private pool is saturated, can we fallback to a hosted lighter model to avoid failures? That's important for our SLAs.
[09:27] Priya Raman: Yup, we support routing policies with fallbacks to either a smaller model or a different region. For strict residency constraints we can limit fallbacks to in-region models only.
[09:38] Ben Park: For the pilot we'd want to run synthetic traffic that mimics the market opening spikes. Can Redwood simulate a 3x spike and measure tail latency and CPU/GPU saturation?
[09:47] Jonah Mills: Absolutely. For the lab we'll run stress tests with stepped loads and capture p99/p999 latencies and token throughput. We'll also test KV cache hit rates and behavior on cold starts.
[09:59] Sara Kim: Questions from security: 1) Do you provide audit logs that are immutable? 2) Is admin access logged to our SIEM? 3) Are there SOC2 controls for change management for the runtime?
[10:10] Alex Chen: 1) We can ship append-only audit logs with digests to S3 with versioning enabled. 2) Admin actions are logged and we can forward them to your SIEM. 3) Yes, our private deployments are subject to the same change management policies; we'll provide evidence and runbooks.
[10:24] Mark Holloway: Will you share an example bucket policy and least-privilege IAM role for the data-plane instances?
[10:29] Priya Raman: We'll attach a sample Terraform and IAM set in the follow-ups.
[10:34] Alex Chen: Quick note: we'll also include a sample CloudFormation for PrivateLink and Transit Gateway attachments.
[10:40] Ben Park: About region constraints again — some EU customers restrict any management plane metadata leaving the EU. Is it realistic to host the control plane in eu-central-1 for just a subset of customers?
[10:51] Jonah Mills: Yes, we can run control planes per-region; for enterprise customers we can create a region-dedicated control plane in eu-central-1 that only touches EU tenants. That increases operational cost but meets residency needs.
[11:04] Sara Kim: Is that an extra contract line item?
[11:07] Alex Chen: Typically yes — region-dedicated control plane is an enterprise add-on. We'll outline pricing with the follow-up.
[11:14] Mark Holloway: Regarding private endpoints, how do you provision them? Is it self-service from our Console or an infra ticket to Redwood?
[11:22] Priya Raman: Initially it's infra-assisted — Redwood provisions the endpoint and you approve the accept. For large installs we can offer IaC modules so you can self-provision.
[11:31] Lina Ortega: Ok. A couple of gotchas: our egress goes through a central NAT for cost accounting; we need egress IP mapping to that NAT. Will that break anything?
[11:41] Jonah Mills: No, as long as you host the data plane inside your NAT, the outbound IP is your NAT. If you use managed egress we need to coordinate so the public egress IPs map to firewall rules.
[11:53] Ben Park: Bandwidth metering question: can we see per-route token counts and bytes so we can attribute costs?
[11:59] Priya Raman: Yes, Redwood Console provides token and byte-level attribution per route, per model, and per token type. You can export CSVs or push metrics to your Prometheus.
[12:10] Mark Holloway: That helps for billing back to business units.
[12:14] Alex Chen: We'll include a screenshot of the console in the follow-up so you can see the token breakdown and cost per model.
[12:21] Mark Holloway: Let's pivot to disaster recovery: if a region fails, what's your recommended DR approach to avoid violating data residency?
[12:30] Jonah Mills: Options: 1) Active-active in two in-region AZs (preferred), 2) Warm standby in a secondary region with replication, with the caveat that you may need legal and compliance approval for cross-region failovers. We'll document RTO/RPO options.
[12:47] Lina Ortega: For financial data we probably want warm standby in the same legal boundary or have predefined failover rules that require explicit approval.
[12:56] Sara Kim: How do you do encryption at rest for cached KV data?
[13:00] Priya Raman: KV cache can be encrypted with customer-provided keys and stored on encrypted volumes. Snapshots can be encrypted as well.
[13:07] Ben Park: Any special requirements for our hardware? We plan to use p4d-equivalent nodes for GPU. Does Redwood runtime have specific CUDA or driver versions?
[13:16] Jonah Mills: We'll provide exact driver/kernel and CUDA versions in the install doc. We tend to support a matrix of modern drivers; for p4d or equivalent we'll confirm matching versions during pilot.
[13:28] Mark Holloway: Another practical: how do you do upgrades? We can't have automatic restarts that break in-progress sessions.
[13:34] Priya Raman: Upgrades are rolling with health checks. You can schedule maintenance windows and we support canary upgrades and traffic drift to minimize impact. We'll include a maintenance policy.
[13:47] Alex Chen: Ok, we have about 35 minutes left — any deeper technical items we should call out for the pilot?
[13:53] Ben Park: PVC: do you require persistent volumes for KV? How large will those be?
[13:57] Jonah Mills: KV cache is in-memory for the GPU processes, but we use persistent disk for checkpoints and snapshotting; size depends on model and KV policy. For 7B models with 1M token KV, you'd provision tens to hundreds of GB. We'll estimate in the sizing doc.
[14:13] Mark Holloway: For the pilot we want a checklist so our network team can pre-stage firewall rules etc. Can you provide a checklist of ports, IPs, and IaC snippets?
[14:20] Alex Chen: Yes, checklist will be in the follow-up along with Terraform samples.
[14:25] Priya Raman: Quick note on autoscaling: we can scale by tokens/sec or by queue depth and tune cold-start behavior. For your spike profile tokens/sec scaling is usually better.
[14:37] Ben Park: Does scaling spin up new GPUs or reuse warm workers?
[14:40] Jonah Mills: Both. We prefer warm pools for latency-sensitive bursts and spin new infra for longer sustained loads.
[14:48] Lina Ortega: Ok let's talk fail-closed vs fail-open behavior. If your Private runtime loses connectivity to Redwood control plane, do calls still flow through?
[14:58] Priya Raman: If you self-host the control plane in your VPC, traffic continues. If you're using Redwood-managed control plane and there's an outage, we have fallback policies — you can choose fail-closed to stop requests or fail-open to route to a local cached model if available.
[15:13] Mark Holloway: We would likely want fail-closed for sensitive customers.
[15:16] Alex Chen: Noted. We'll make that configurable per-route.
[15:21] Ben Park: Any recommended monitoring thresholds for alerts? CPU/GPU util, queue depth, and p99 latency?
[15:26] Jonah Mills: Yes: GPU util > 80% sustained, queue depth spikes over baseline, p99 latency above SLA. We'll provide sample Prometheus alert rules.
[15:36] Sara Kim: A non-technical ask: can we get references from similar financial customers who've done Private deployments?
[15:42] Alex Chen: We can share anonymized references and case studies — I'll get legal to sign an NDA if needed for specifics.
[15:50] Mark Holloway: Ok, near the end — let's recap next steps.
[15:53] Alex Chen: Recap: 1) Alex sends SOC2, network diagram, ACLs, IaC samples by 2026-10-07. 2) Ben provides egress IP list and bandwidth baseline by 2026-10-09. 3) Priya prepares sizing and quant recommendations for pilot by 2026-10-12. 4) Schedule lab benchmark for week of 2026-10-13. Anything else?
[16:12] Mark Holloway: That covers it. Also include cost model for Private-hosted vs Dedicated by next touch.
[16:19] Alex Chen: We'll include a cost model.
[16:22] Jonah Mills: I'll add an appendix to the pilot plan describing how we simulate your opening spikes and what metrics we'll capture.
[16:29] Ben Park: Thanks — also please include minimal IAM roles so we can pre-provision.
[16:33] Priya Raman: On it.
[16:35] Lina Ortega: Final note: our procurement timeline is tight so sooner the better.
[16:41] Alex Chen: Understood. We'll move quickly. Thanks all for your time.
[16:46] Mark Holloway: Thank you.
[16:48] Sara Kim: Thanks.

[End of recording — remaining time was Q&A off-line]
